collection.description: They're standing on the beach, each holding the other's shell.

ask.text:
(subject) and (friend) have each found half of a rare double shell, a pair that fit together perfectly, and they've had them carved into necklaces. An old carver tells them that in the old days, friends who swapped such shells "swapped a little of themselves" too, and that's why it was done at weddings and not between friends.
They're standing on the beach, each holding the other's shell. The carver is watching, frowning.
Should they swap, or keep their own halves?

c1o1.text: They look at each other, and each sees (subject.himself/herself), wearing the other's shell. "A little of themselves," the carver says, sighing. "I did say it was for weddings." They swap the shells back. Nothing changes back with them. In the end they keep each other's lives, and say it's made them better friends than ever.

c1o2.text: Nothing much happens, except that the next morning (subject) wakes up feeling that (subject.his/her) name belongs to someone else now, as if (subject.he/she) gave a little of it away with the shell. (subject.He/She) chooses a new one, and (friend) is the first to use it. The carver says that's about as little as it ever gets.

c1.text: They hang the shells round each other's necks. The two halves click softly against their chests, as if trying to fit back together...

c2o1.text: They walk home, each with half the shell. Whenever they stand together, the halves click softly. They're friends for the rest of their lives, and nobody ever has to swap anything to make it so.

c2o2.text: (subject) has always kept away from village gatherings, too shy to stand in a crowd. But from then on, whenever the village gathers, (subject.he/she) goes, because (friend) will be there, and the shells click when they find each other. (subject.He/She) comes to every festival after that.

c2.text: They look at the carver's face, and at each other, and hang their own shells back round their own necks. The carver nods, relieved...
